summary: Paul Elliott Singer founded Elliott Management in 1977 and built it into a large activist-investment firm. His political influence combines major Republican giving with long leadership of the Manhattan Institute, pro-Israel organizations and a separate record of funding marriage equality, illustrating a donor whose coalition does not fit every social-conservative position.

statements.summary: Singer described his investing worldview as focused on preparing for extreme outcomes that markets systematically underprice.
Singer argued that allowing same-sex couples to marry was consistent with conservative commitments to family and stability.
He warned that unprecedented money creation could eventually undermine confidence in currencies and financial assets.
Singer presented activist investing as a means of forcing boards and managers to confront underperformance and capital allocation.
Elliott framed the Argentina litigation as enforcement of contracts and equal treatment under law.

chapters.title: Law before markets
chapters.dek: A lawyer becomes a risk investor
chapters.body:
Paul Singer was born in Teaneck, New Jersey, in 1944. He studied psychology at Rochester and earned a Harvard law degree before shifting from legal practice into investing [[newyorker-singer-2018, wef-singer]].

Legal training remained central to Elliott's model: contracts, court remedies and willingness to sustain disputes became competitive tools [[institutional-investor-2017]].

chapters.title: Building Elliott
chapters.body:
Singer founded Elliott in 1977 with $1.3 million. The firm grew through distressed debt, event-driven trades and campaigns pressing public-company boards for operational or financial change [[elliott-leadership, forbes-singer-2026]].

Supporters call the strategy accountability for managers and borrowers; critics argue it extracts value through legal and financial pressure. Both descriptions depend on the specific case [[newyorker-singer-2018, institutional-investor-2017]].

chapters.title: The Argentina test
chapters.dek: Contract enforcement against a sovereign state
chapters.body:
Elliott affiliate NML Capital bought defaulted Argentine bonds and refused restructuring terms accepted by most creditors. Years of litigation reached the U.S. Supreme Court and constrained Argentina's access to markets [[supreme-argentina-2014, newyorker-singer-2018]].

Argentina settled in 2016. The outcome demonstrated Elliott's patience and legal leverage while making Singer a global symbol of the dispute over holdout creditors [[reuters-argentina-2016]].

chapters.title: Republican power through outside groups
chapters.body:
Singer supported Romney, Rubio and Haley in successive Republican presidential cycles, often favoring internationalist or establishment candidates [[nyt-marriage-2012, newyorker-singer-2018, ap-haley-2024]].

His more durable spending goes to Senate and House leadership super PACs. Those organizations preserve influence even when his preferred presidential candidate loses [[fec-singer, bloomberg-singer-2026]].

chapters.title: Marriage equality and coalition limits
chapters.dek: A major Republican donor breaks with social conservatives
chapters.body:
Singer became a leading Republican funder of marriage equality, motivated publicly in part by his son's experience. He financed lobbying, campaigns and efforts to give Republican legislators political cover [[nyt-marriage-2012, freedom-marry-singer]].

That work complicates a one-dimensional ideological label but does not make the rest of his conservative funding bipartisan. The relevant record is issue-specific [[fec-singer, nyt-marriage-2012]].

chapters.title: Policy and pro-Israel institutions
chapters.body:
Singer's long chairmanship of the Manhattan Institute supported work on cities, markets, policing and public administration. He also funds Jewish communal and pro-Israel advocacy [[manhattan-board, manhattan-singer, rjc-singer]].

These organizations act independently; a gift establishes support, not control over every publication or position [[manhattan-board]].

chapters.title: Tail risk as worldview
chapters.body:
Singer is known for focusing on outcomes that consensus pricing treats as unlikely. Elliott letters have warned about leverage, monetary expansion and political shocks [[newyorker-singer-2018, fortune-singer-letter-2020]].

The same posture appears in his politics: strong defense, support for Israel and skepticism toward fiscal and monetary policy are framed as preparation for risks institutions underweight [[rjc-singer, manhattan-singer]].

chapters.title: Present influence
chapters.dek: A repeat donor in the 2026 midterms
chapters.body:
Singer remains Elliott's founder, president, co-CEO and co-CIO. Forbes continues to value his fortune in the billions, while Elliott remains private [[elliott-leadership, forbes-singer-2026]].

In 2026 he again directed large sums to congressional leadership groups. The FEC ledger captures those personal checks but not his foundation, policy institutions or the actions of Elliott itself [[bloomberg-singer-2026, fec-singer]].
